extracted.intended_audience: school and institution administrators, Title IX coordinators, higher- and elementary/secondary-education legal counsel, and policymakers implementing Title IX regulations
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble discussion and final-regulation decisions about the §106.30 definition of sexual harassment, including inclusion of sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking, how consent and related elements are to be treated, and related procedural guidance for recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking in §106.30
rubrics_metrics.description: Revises the third prong of the final §106.30 definition of sexual harassment to add, after sexual assault, dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking as defined in VAWA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department was persuaded that dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking are inherently serious sex-based offenses that risk equal educational access and therefore should not always be subjected to the Davis "severe and pervasive" standard. The final regulations include these offenses alongside sexual assault so that recipients must respond to them under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual assault included as a form of sexual harassment (Clery Act/Statute reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third prong of §106.30 references "sexual assault" per the Clery Act (now referenced by statute) as part of the definition of sexual harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including sexual assault is not an empty reference—the Department will enforce each part of §106.30 and require recipients to respond to sexual assault. The Department views the Clery Act statutory reference as appropriately broad, capturing forcible and non-forcible sex offenses as defined by the FBI UCR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Davis standard (second prong) — severity/pervasiveness/equal-access
rubrics_metrics.description: The second prong of the §106.30 definition uses the Davis standard: unwelcome conduct on the basis of sex determined by a reasonable person to be so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively denies a person equal access to the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes that some offenses (e.g., dating violence, domestic violence, stalking) may not always meet this severity/pervasiveness test if incidents are considered discretely, which is why those offenses are also included in the third prong. The Davis elements remain the test for the second prong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quid pro quo (first prong)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first prong concerns an employee of the recipient conditioning the provision of an educational aid, benefit, or service on an individual's participation in unwelcome sexual conduct (quid pro quo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any individual may experience quid pro quo sexual harassment; it is covered by the §106.30 definition and recipients must respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual assault treated as inherently serious; denial of equal access not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Because courts have reached different conclusions about whether a single rape meets the Davis standard, the Department includes single instances of sexual assault as actionable under §106.30 and declines to require a separate "denial of equal access" element for sexual assault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual assault is considered to inherently create a serious, sex-based impediment to equal access to education that Title IX is designed to prohibit; therefore single incidents are actionable without needing additional proof of denial of equal access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Clery Act and VAWA statutes (harmonization and stability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations reference sexual assault via the Clery Act statute and reference dating violence, domestic violence, and stalking via the VAWA statutes rather than citing to the Clery Act regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach harmonizes Clery Act and Title IX obligations for postsecondary institutions, provides elementary and secondary schools a federal reference, and reduces vulnerability to changes in Clery Act regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fondling requires a "purpose of sexual gratification" element
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Clery Act/FBI UCR definition, fondling is the touching of a person's private body parts without the consent of the victim for purposes of sexual gratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This "purpose" requirement distinguishes sexualized fondling from incidental or non-sexual touching (e.g., jostling or children playing doctor). For juveniles, recipients should examine circumstances like age and maturity before ascribing a sexualized purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempts included in sexual assault (FBI UCR treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The FBI has stated that the offense of rape includes attempts to commit rape; the Clery Act/FBI UCR framework therefore captures attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department relies on the FBI UCR's inclusion of attempts to ensure attempted sexual assault falls within the sexual assault category under §106.30.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients retain flexibility to define consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department intentionally leaves recipients flexibility and discretion to craft their own definitions of consent (and related terms describing absence or negation of consent, such as coercion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will not require recipients to adopt a particular definition of consent; a recipient should select a definition that best serves its community's needs, values, and environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may address conduct outside of Title IX via other codes of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that does not meet the §106.30 definition of sexual harassment (but may still be harmful) can be addressed by recipients under non-Title IX codes of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain discretion to set standards of conduct beyond Title IX and to address less-serious misconduct that could escalate into actionable harassment if left unaddressed. The Department declines to prohibit recipients from doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural discretion and protections in the §106.45 grievance process
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations provide procedural pathways: recipients may facilitate informal resolution after a formal complaint; Title IX Coordinators are not mandated to file formal complaints upon multiple reports; formal complaints may be dismissed if complainant withdraws; disciplinary sanctions are not prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural provisions aim to prevent recipients from being forced to pursue Title IX processes for situations where parties did not find conduct unwelcome and to ensure fairness and robust procedural protections for complainants and respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declining to adopt alternative narrower definitions of sexual assault
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines commenters' proposed alternative definitions (e.g., state-law-by-state or FBI NIBRS-only approaches) and believes the Clery Act/VAWA/FBI UCR references appropriately capture a broad range of sex offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department considers the Clery Act/VAWA statutory references sufficiently broad and consistent across jurisdictions to serve Title IX purposes without imposing a new federal definition of consent or other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of statutory rape and incest within sexual assault
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to exclude incest and statutory rape from the definition of sexual assault, recognizing established circumstances in which consent cannot legally be given (e.g., underage parties, familial prohibitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where sexual activity meets a definition of sexual assault under §106.30—even if parties appear willing—recipients have flexibility regarding whether to pursue formal complaints, informal resolution, or other disciplinary avenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual harassment protections apply irrespective of sexual orientation or gender identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The three-prong definition of sexual harassment applies to any individual—irrespective of sexual orientation or gender identity—who is victimized by the covered conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that Title IX's prohibition on discrimination "on the basis of sex" covers harassment and assault of LGBTQ individuals; the rules do not exclude victims based on orientation or gender identity even though the statute does not define "sex."

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of statutory presupposition of binary sex; Department declines to define "sex"
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX and some implementing provisions presuppose sex as a binary classification in certain statutory text; the Department did not propose and declines to adopt a definition of "sex" in the final regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department incorporates the statutory phrase "on the basis of sex" in its definition of sexual harassment but leaves the meaning of "sex" undefined in the regulatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarding against vague/overbroad definitions and ensuring fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters expressed concern that vague, overbroad sexual misconduct policies have resulted in unfair punishments for respondents and denied complainants meaningful participation; the Department acknowledges these concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For that reason the Department prescribes the §106.45 grievance process to provide robust procedural protections for both complainants and respondents and encourages recipients to adopt clear definitions and processes while retaining discretion to address conduct outside Title IX.
